content: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) is a prevalent condition among adolescents and young adults, characterized by pain located behind or around the patella. This pain is often accompanied by crepitus and is exacerbated by activities such as ascending or descending stairs, squatting, prolonged sitting with flexed knees, running, and cycling. These symptoms can significantly impair daily activities and sports performance. Pharmacological treatments for PFPS are primarily aimed at alleviating pain or addressing presumed underlying pathologies. Commonly used medications include non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and glucocorticosteroids for pain relief, as well as compounds like glucosamine to promote cartilage metabolism and anabolic steroids to enhance patellar bone density and strengthen supporting musculature. In clinical studies, these pharmacological interventions are often combined with exercise programs designed to build supporting muscle strength. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of pharmacotherapy in reducing anterior knee pain and improving knee function in individuals with PFPS. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, was conducted to identify relevant studies up to January 2004. The review included controlled trials, both randomized and non-randomized, that compared pharmacotherapy with placebo, other pharmacological treatments, or non-pharmacological therapies in patients with PFPS. The search yielded 780 publications, of which eight trials met the inclusion criteria. Three of these trials were deemed to be of high quality. Due to variability in drug administration routes, care programs, and outcome measures, a meta-analysis was not feasible, and the data were instead analyzed qualitatively using a best evidence synthesis approach. Four trials, involving a total of 163 participants, investigated the effects of NSAIDs. A high-quality trial comparing aspirin to placebo found no significant differences in clinical symptoms or signs. Naproxen demonstrated significant short-term pain reduction compared to placebo but showed no significant advantage over diflunisal. Laser therapy, aimed at stimulating blood flow in tender areas, resulted in higher participant satisfaction compared to tenoxicam, although the difference was not statistically significant. Two high-quality randomized controlled trials, involving 84 participants, examined the effects of glycosaminoglycan polysulphate (GAGPS). Twelve intramuscular injections administered over six weeks led to a significantly higher proportion of participants reporting a good overall therapeutic effect after one year, as well as significantly better pain reduction during one of two assessed activities. Another study compared five weekly intra-articular injections of GAGPS and lidocaine with intra-articular saline and lidocaine injections or no injections, all combined with quadriceps training. Participants who received injections showed improved function after six weeks, but only the difference between the GAGPS group and the non-injected group was statistically significant. However, these differences were no longer evident after one year. One trial, involving 43 participants, evaluated the effects of intramuscular injections of the anabolic steroid nandrolone phenylpropionate. This intervention significantly improved both pain and function compared to placebo injections. In conclusion, there is limited evidence supporting the effectiveness of NSAIDs for short-term pain relief in PFPS. The evidence regarding glycosaminoglycan polysulphate is inconsistent and warrants further investigation. While the anabolic steroid nandrolone phenylpropionate may show promise in improving pain and function, its use remains controversial and is not widely accepted as a treatment for PFPS.
